did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a request that the LORD himself stand beside the psalmist in his struggle: “Contend, LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me.” In this way, the LORD is portrayed as the protector who takes up the cause of the persecuted.
Did you know? Verses 2–3 mention weapons from the ancient world—a shield, a large shield, and a spear. The psalmist uses these images to ask for active protection and deliverance from his pursuers.

Did you know? Verses 4–6 describe the defeat of those seeking his harm through images of retreat, shame, chaff blown by the wind, darkness, and a slippery path. The enemies are depicted through a combination of battle imagery and images of danger and losing one’s way.

Did you know? The word “without cause” is repeated in verses 7–8: the enemies set a net and dug a pit for him without justification, and the psalmist asks that their own trap ensnare them. This reflects the principle of measure-for-measure justice as presented in the psalm.

Did you know? After describing the danger, the tone changes: the psalmist declares, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD.” Joy and thanksgiving are presented here as the result of deliverance, and in verse 10 he emphasizes that the LORD saves the poor and needy from the powerful and the one who robs them.

Did you know? Verses 11–16 describe a response of ingratitude: people bring forward malicious witnesses and repay the psalmist evil for good. By contrast, he recalls that he mourned for them, wore sackcloth, and fasted when they were in trouble, while they rejoiced when he stumbled.

Did you know? The psalmist’s plea, “Lord, how long will you look on?” emphasizes that, in his view, the LORD sees the injustice but has not yet intervened. He immediately asks for deliverance from the enemies, who are vividly portrayed as lions threatening his life.

Did you know? The psalmist promises to thank the LORD not only in private but also “in the great assembly” and among “a mighty people.” Thanksgiving for deliverance is meant to be a public testimony, not merely a personal experience.

Did you know? In the final part of the psalm, the psalmist also confronts mockery and malicious gloating: he asks that his enemies not wink at one another or say, “Aha!” when they see his distress. He then asks for open judgment, shame for the evildoers, and joy for those who love justice, concluding with a commitment to speak of the LORD’s righteousness and praise him all day long.
